Director of Engineering here at the City of Kitchener.
We're here to present the final outcome.
We're here to present the final outcome of the Bean Drive and Sanitary Sewer Assessment.
Bean Drive is located in Ward 4, found to the south of Huron Road in the Brigadoon neighbourhood.
It was constructed in 1986.
Much of this neighbourhood was constructed at the same time.
Bean was planned, designed and built as a major collector road and is identified as
such in our official plan.
More-South traffic coming through this area currently utilizes Bean Drive and Carrendale
Drive, which is classified as a minor collector road.
A minor collector compared to a major collector primarily deals with the differences in actual
use.
Where a major collector balances mobility of people between neighbourhoods, a minor collector
prioritizes active neighbourhood life and facilitates movement within neighbourhoods.
An extension of Bean Drive has long been considered.
A need has been identified in numerous planning documents and community plans.
The project has been included in our D.C. background study and our budget since 2009.
Timing for the project has ultimately been dependent, pending further developments to the south.
The project requires that an environmental assessment be completed.
This was initiated in March of 2021 and was conducted to evaluate and determine if there is a need for extending the road
and evaluating solutions for that.
An EA is a provincial planning process for public infrastructure projects in Ontario.
They are governed by the Ontario Environmental Assessment Act.
An EA provides framework for assessing the impacts of a project on the natural,
socioeconomic and cultural environments and provides the public, stakeholders and agencies
to provide feedback and input into decision-making processes.
One of the first tasks while completing an EA is to develop a problem or opportunity statement.
This defines the problem that is trying to be solved and becomes a measuring stick that
alternatives are evaluated against.
For this EA, our problem statement focused on transportation needs and whether a road
extension was necessary.
It is important to note that through the course of completing the EA, the problem statement
was slightly modified.
This was done to ensure that the need for the road was not something that was predetermined.
The project was started in March of 2021.
Studies and evaluations were completed.
There were two public presentations of the project, one to introduce the project and
the other to present the findings.
Public stakeholder and agency comments were received and considered and the report and
evaluation finalized and presented to Council in February of 2023.
The preferred alternative at that time was to extend Bean Drive to connect to the future
Robert Ferry Drive extension.
A decision on the EA at that time was deferred, and staff were asked to complete two additional
studies.
An updated transportation study that would reconsider the impacts of Robert Ferry Drive
extension and a new geotechnical investigation.
The studies were completed and incorporated into the study and evaluations of alternatives.
The results were presented to the public at a PIC in June of 2024, and the alternatives
in the final report were finalized.
Since we were last at Council, we completed the two studies.
We've addressed changes to species at risk classifications, adjusted our alternatives
to separate the need for the road from the sewer and water main, adjusted our scoring
matrix to provide a more transparent scoring.
We hosted the third public information session, engaged with an independent consultant to
review our project processes, and circulated the final document to the ministry for review
and then addressed any of their comments in our final report.
While traffic volumes alone do not warrant the extension of Bean, the updated transportation
study returned a recommendation to extend the road.
The future extension of Robert Ferry and Strasburg Road will likely redistribute traffic
volumes on Carrendale, leaving it functioning as a major community collector street. Carrendale
is best served as a minor collector based on the existing design details and the presence
of a school in the corridor. Extending Bean also addresses insufficient emergency access
at the end of Bean that currently exists. It provides a proper distribution of traffic
to a greater area, and it provides a proper transportation linkage to the south in all
of our future development in that area. The geotechnical study confirmed
feasibility of trenchless pipe installation. So based on the geotechnical
investigation, we should be able to install the sewer and the water main
trenchlessly. This means that the sewer doesn't need the road construction to be
installed and we were able to revise our alternatives as such. We revised our
alternatives and carried a new do-nothing alternative, which is to install the
utilities with no road. Additionally, we carried through a new option of including a trail
in lieu of a road. We evaluated four options. There were five factors that are included
in the scoring matrix. Transportation, which includes things like emergency response, school
safety and support of our transportation master plans. Natural environment, which includes
wildlife habitat, species at risk, and groundwater, socioeconomic, which addresses disruption
to different parts of the neighbourhood, land use, which supports our official plan and capital
construction costs.
Extension of the road scored the most favourable.
This was followed by installing the utilities with no road, with the multi-use trail option
being our fourth preferred alternative.
It is key to note that with the do-nothing alternative, it does nothing to remedy overall
area transportation issues.
Without being extended, Carindill Drive will continue to function as a major collector
road when Robert Ferry is extended.
This is a road classification different than designated.
It does not fully address all concerns identified as part of the study.
The two road extension alternatives are recommended in the updated transportation study, and it
It holds true to current and historical planning for the area.
It additionally addresses the existing emergency access issue for Bean Drive.
While this carries a road through a provincially significant wetland, impacts can be mitigated.
For example, we are proposing a compensation of wetland disturbance at a two-to-one rate.
A trail or multi-use path was evaluated in lieu of a road.
While this would provide a really nice active transportation link and could remedy the emergency
services deficiency, it does not address the vehicle trip distribution, and without road
appearances, it causes as much ecological impacts as a road would.
Our preferred alternative, which is the best-balanced solution, providing the best performance while
balancing natural, socioeconomic and financial impacts, includes the removal of the temporary
cul-de-sac at the end of Bean Drive. It extends a two-lane road through to the future Robert
Ferry Drive extension. It passes through a forested wetland and through a planned development.
This road will include pedestrian and active transportation facilities and wildlife mitigations
like exclusion fencing, wildlife crossings, and wetland compensation. This option includes
the installation of the trunk sewer and water main.
With Council endorsement, the EA will be filed for its 30-day commenting period and then
be finalized.
Pending completion of this, the project will advance to the detailed design phase, securing
of permits, tendering and then construction.
Permitting for this project will be extensive.
It includes permits related to species at risk and construction dewatering.
there are several environmental timing windows for construction that will need to be adhered to as
well. Construction would not begin until 2026 at the earliest. As recommended, this project would
improve accessibility to the local community. It defines a multimodal transportation plan within
existing and future neighborhoods, and it allows for development to proceed on lands that require
the infrastructure. This project has been completed by a well-experienced engineering consultant.
All studies in supporting work was completed by qualified professionals.
This project followed a provincial process.
We have had the document reviewed by the Ministry and have had a third-party consultant review
the processes that were followed.
I'll note, Council cannot change the alternatives that are included in this study, nor can Council
choose a different preferred alternative.
We are asking Council to support the filing of this EA as presented.
Thank you.

Council members, tonight I'm going to talk about the impact of traffic on Carondale Drive
from a neighbourhood point of view.
For 36 years I've lived on Carondale Drive near Brigadoon School and for the last three
years, I, along with area residents, have been actively opposing the city's plan to extend
Bean Drive to Robert Ferry. Why? Because this extension will do nothing to move traffic around.
In 1989, notice was given to residents that Bean would be extended to Strasbourg.
Robert Ferry to Strasbourg was not part of the equation, as Bean was planned to be the direct
route to Strasbourg. We now know that plans have changed to have Robert Ferry meet Strasbourg
road due to the significant growth in Dune South. The original plan to extend Bean was
well intended as an efficient route for Brigadoon residents to travel to Strasbourg, but over
the years significant environmental concerns were raised and challenged as noted in the
EA. The City's new proposals that Bean be extended to Robert Ferry, a much shorter road
through a soggy wetland. The reality is extending Robert Ferry to Strasbourg has replaced the
need for the Bean extension. The majority of traffic on Carrendale and Bean today is
coming from Dune South, not from residents living in this part of Brigadoon. Proceeding
with the Bean Drive extension will require costly special engineering of the road and
additional costs to maintain it for a road that will serve very few homes. In September,
I spoke with Paradigm for about 45 minutes about the upcoming traffic studies they were
doing in our area. I emphasized to them that the traffic would feel heavy on both Carrendale
and Bean because these streets were currently being used as a bypass by Dune South residents
when travelling west to Strasburg and Huron Roads. I emphasised that it was critical to
measure the vehicles coming to and from the Dune South community via Robert Ferry Drive.
The intent of this request was to measure the traffic patterns of Dune South residents
using Carondale and Bean as their bypass to Strasburg Road as the Robert Ferry extension
had not yet been completed.
I assure you that Paradigm understood my concerns, but their new studies ultimately did not measure
these statistics, but simply counted cars.
How can the city use flawed data to reliably project future traffic patterns on Carondale
and Bean?
I walk the area a lot and estimate conservatively that at least 50% of the traffic on Carondale
and Bean is coming from Dune South.
Since Robert Ferry is extended, along with the planned Blair Creek extension, Dune South
residents will be able to take one of these two roads to Strasbourg, removing a huge volume
of traffic on Carondale and Bean.
Now to the safety concerns near Brigadoon School.
Much has been done by the city to increase the safety of children walking to and from
school.
Traffic calming measures on Carondale include two places where the road narrows to allow
pedestrians to cross safely, eliminating the dangers I personally saw of children crossing
Carrendale at Robertson years ago. Most students are accompanied by adults, which adds an extra
layer of safety. Our strong recommendation is to go with the do-nothing, along with alternative
four as outlined in the EA. Residents living in the west end of Brigadoon would use Carrendale
to access Robert Ferry to go west to Strasburg Road. Dune South residents, on the other hand,
remain on Robert Ferry to access Strasbourg Road, allowing for traffic counts on Carondale
and Bean to reduce significantly and be well below the allotment of expected vehicles.
City staff continuously reiterate the perception of a future traffic problem that they say
must be solved by extending Bean Drive. We're absolutely confident that the proposed Bean
Drive extension won't impact or reroute traffic at all. Rather, this short road extension
will be redundant and a total waste of development charges that could be allocated for other
infrastructure projects or cost overruns, notwithstanding the annual maintenance costs of the road extension
because of its special design. Not proceeding with this extension will also eliminate our
concerns with the wildlife who roam in the area and whom we keep pushing out of our green
spaces due to development. In closing, we respectfully ask you to fully
consider the Alternative 4 along with the do-nothing as a solution along with the recommended trenchless
installation for the sanitary and sewer services as this alternative makes for smart development.
It will allow the developers to proceed when ready and allow for the completion of Robert
Ferry. Clearly a three-way win for the residents, wildlife and overall environment, for the
city to save on development charges and apply elsewhere, and for the respective developers
to proceed with building new homes.
The solution really doesn't get any better than that.
I thank you for your consideration and for your time tonight.
Thank you.
Thank you, Ms. Cusack.
Don't see any questions for you.
Thank you very much.

Hello, everyone. Thank you for taking the time to listen to my delegation. My name is
Ray Angod and today I'd like to discuss the traffic aspect of the proposed Beanline extension.
The messaging about this project has been very consistent. The Bean Drive extension
would be a major collector road and would help mitigate cut-through traffic on local
streets within the community.
I reviewed the recently released ESR to better understand this position and I found something
surprising.
The authors claim a daily trip generation rate of almost 10, which they convert directly
into vehicle trips.
Based on this, they estimate a total of over 11,000 vehicle trips from these 1,200 residences.
This doesn't make intuitive sense to me, and I would like you to think about this in
real-life terms.
What's being suggested here is that for each household, a vehicle leaves, returns, leaves,
returns, leaves, returns, leaves, returns, leaves, returns.
Every household, every single day.
As fellow Kitchener residents, does this match your understanding of how often the average
community member drives?
If we compare this with a comparable Mississauga study, which also uses trip generation rates,
they show their work to estimate 159 two-way trips during peak hours for 207 residences,
which is a much more intuitive result.
Not only are the traffic volumes surprising, but so are the traffic flows.
Here, it's suggested that 90% of all vehicle traffic in this neighbourhood will take the Bean Drive extension,
with no explanation how they got this number of 90%.
This seems unintuitive, because the most common destinations are in the opposite direction of this road extension.
Contrast that with the Mississauga study, where they performed local traffic pattern modeling
to estimate more balanced traffic flows. So I was not content with the conclusions in the ESR,
so I set out to accurately measure the expected traffic patterns. And my methodology was simple.
I measured the distance from representative sample of origins where people live
to the nearest major intersection, the destination of Huron and Strasbourg,
and determine which routes would have the shortest distance via the Bean Drive extension.
And here's an example.
So this is Bean and Spencer, one of the origins,
and I measured the distance getting to Huron and Strasburg using Moral Meadow.
It's 1.88 kilometers.
I measured the same origin to destination using the Bean Drive extension,
and it's longer, 2.39 kilometers.
I measured the distance from each origin to the destination via four different routes.
The shortest route for each origin is highlighted in green.
You'll notice that the Bean Drive extension is not the shortest route for any of these
representative origins.
Based on this distance study, the impact of the Bean Drive extension on alleviating traffic
should be considered negligible.
Now a case could be made for measuring speed instead of distance, so I investigated that
as well.
Let's go back to my original measurement of Bean and Spencer to Huron and Strasburg.
If you compensate for speed, then the Bean Drive extension would be up to 24 seconds faster.
The question is, how many residences would benefit?
I measured that these 95 households with a green checkmark would benefit from faster travel times,
and the average time saved for these 95 households would be about 12 seconds.
I took it one step further and calculated the payback period, which is the amount of
time it would take for this road extension to pay for itself.
I made a few assumptions up top, but the bottom line is, if each of these 95 residences take
four vehicle trips to Huron and Strasbourg every single day, a total of $10,000 would
be saved each year.
Contrast that with the road construction costs of about $7.5 million, which does not include
the sewer costs.
Even if we assume an interest rate of zero, the payback period for this project is about
730 years.
Much greater than I imagine is the expected lifespan of this road.
To conclude, the data suggests that the Bean Drive extension cannot be justified from a
traffic perspective.
This delegation recommends Alternative 4 and the accelerated approval of the Robert
Fair extension to Strasbourg.
Thank you.
Thank you, Mr. Ingood.
I don't see any questions.
Thank you.
